title: Scheduler instrumentation: queueing time + batch-size distribution for perf canary attribution
creator: Noah Patel
description:
We need scheduler-level instrumentation to attribute observed perf regressions (p95 latency/tokens/sec) to:
- queueing/backpressure (scheduler waiting, admission control, pool saturation)
- execution/runtime time (prefill/decode, kernel selection, KV cache)

This ticket adds and validates queueing-time metrics in the serving scheduler and ensures they can be consumed by perf-canary dashboards/alerts with safe label cardinality.

Context:
Perf canary will run synthetic prompts continuously. When it detects p95 regressions, on-call needs immediate signal whether the issue is:
- fleet/capacity (queueing time up)
- runtime execution (execution time up)
- batching behavior shift (batch size distribution changes)

Deliverable: emit scheduler queueing-time metrics + batch-size distribution with consistent units/labels, and validate correctness under load.

Links:
- Project design (Confluence): sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/perf-regression-canary-design.json
- Metric definitions ticket: ENG-4873
- Runtime telemetry tags: PR planned in redwood repo (see implementation notes)
- Cardinality audit memo (Drive): sources/google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/observability/perf-canary-metrics-cardinality-audit.json
acceptance_criteria:
1) Queueing time is measured at scheduler boundary (request admitted -> dispatched to execution) and emitted as a histogram with ms units.
2) Metrics include enough dimensions for canary attribution without causing cardinality blowups.
3) Dashboard queries can cleanly compute: e2e latency = queueing + execution (+ network where applicable), and p95 queueing trends per model.
4) Validation demonstrates metrics are directionally correct under controlled load (queueing grows as pool saturates).
5) Metrics are emitted for both hosted + dedicated pools (where scheduler is in path) with consistent naming.
6) No customer prompt content is emitted/logged; only timing + safe identifiers.
implementation_notes:
Proposed measurement points (scheduler service):
- t_enqueue: when request is accepted into scheduler queue (post-auth, post-request-shaping), before admission control.
- t_admit: when request is admitted into a batch formation group / runnable set.
- t_dispatch: when request is dispatched to runtime worker (GPU executor) / batch is handed off.

Primary metric (per request):
- scheduler_queueing_ms = t_dispatch - t_enqueue

Optional secondary metrics (useful for attribution, gated by cardinality budget):
- scheduler_admission_ms = t_admit - t_enqueue (time spent blocked by admission control / quotas)
- scheduler_batch_formation_ms = t_dispatch - t_admit (time spent waiting to form a batch)

Batch metrics:
- scheduler_batch_size (histogram or summary): batch size at dispatch time
- scheduler_active_batches (gauge): current number of active batches/executors
- scheduler_queue_depth (gauge): queued requests count

Label set (agreed with Telemetry team to avoid blowups):
- model_id: canonical model identifier (from model registry; stable)
- model_version: optional; include only if already being emitted elsewhere for canary baselines (otherwise omit)
- region: low cardinality
- capacity_tier: hosted|dedicated|private (private only if instrumentation exists)
- hw_sku: A100-80G|H100-80G|L40S etc (bounded set)
- runtime_build_id: handled by separate ticket/PR; do not add to scheduler metrics until cardinality reviewed

Explicitly NOT adding:
- customer_id / org_id / request_id
- prompt_len_bucket labels (canary can supply shapes; runtime metrics should remain generic)

Metric naming (align with existing conventions):
- redwood_scheduler_queueing_ms_bucket (histogram)
- redwood_scheduler_queue_depth (gauge)
- redwood_scheduler_batch_size_bucket (histogram)

Histogram buckets:
- queueing_ms: [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000]
- batch_size: [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64] (cap at scheduler max)

Guardrails:
- All metrics emitted via shared aggregation helper (see PR mention in ENG-4873) to ensure units/hist types are consistent.
- Metrics must be emitted in the scheduler only once per request (avoid double-count in retries). For retries, set a separate counter redwood_scheduler_retry_total (optional follow-up).

Code pointers:
- Scheduler path: request enqueue -> admission control -> batcher -> dispatch to executor.
- Ensure enqueue timestamp is monotonic (steady clock) to prevent NTP skew artifacts.

Rollout:
- Ship behind feature flag: scheduler.queue_metrics_enabled
- Enable in staging at 100% and in prod at 10% for 24h, then 100% after validating metric volume + correctness.

Related PRs:
- sources/github/redwood/pr-19188-runtime-export-queueing-time-metrics.json (primary implementation)
- sources/slack/eng-runtime/1769202109-scheduler-queue-metric-validation.json (validation thread)
- sources/slack/eng-platform/1768611133-metrics-cardinality-review.json (cardinality discussion)
test_plan:
1) Unit tests:
- scheduler_queueing_ms computed from monotonic timestamps
- retry path does not double-emit hist entries

2) Load test in staging (benchmark-lab):
- Generate controlled QPS ramp until GPU executor saturates.
- Verify:
  a) queue_depth increases with QPS
  b) p95 scheduler_queueing_ms increases with QPS
  c) execution latency remains comparatively stable until runtime becomes bottleneck

3) Canary comparison:
- Run perf-canary synthetic workload against staging endpoint.
- Validate: e2e p95 ~= p95(queueing + execution) within tolerance (ack that percentiles don’t add perfectly; compare distributions via sampled traces).

4) Cardinality audit:
- Confirm label values stay within expected bounds (region/hw_sku/capacity_tier/model_id).
- Confirm no request identifiers leak into labels.

5) Dashboard readiness:
- Ensure Grafana panels can break down p95 e2e vs p95 queueing vs p95 execution with consistent units and legends.
risk_and_mitigations:
Risks:
- Incorrect queueing measurement due to measuring at wrong boundary (e.g., includes runtime execution).
- NTP/time skew producing negative/erratic durations.
- Metric volume increase from histograms impacting telemetry cost.
- Cardinality blowups if model_version or runtime_build_id added prematurely.

Mitigations:
- Use monotonic clock.
- Keep queueing metric limited to scheduler-only boundary.
- Bucket carefully; avoid per-request labels.
- Stage rollout with volume checks and coordinate with Telemetry team on retention/downsampling.

comments: 2026-01-08 (Sofia Ivanova): Please make sure “queueing” is strictly scheduler time, not including runtime backpressure after dispatch. In our code, dispatch returns when we hand off to executor queue; that’s the boundary we want.

2026-01-09 (Logan Wright): +1 on monotonic clock. Also: do NOT add request_id, batch_id, or kernel_id labels. Model_id/region/hw_sku/capacity_tier is OK. Model_version only if we can guarantee boundedness.

2026-01-15 (Nadia Rahman): Histogram buckets look good. For queueing_ms, please include up to 5s; we’ve seen pathological cases during fleet incidents. We’ll downsample older data; keep the label set small so we can retain 14d at full res.

2026-01-22 (Omar El-Sayed): Found that enqueue time is currently recorded pre-auth in one path and post-auth in another. Normalizing to post-auth/post-shaping so it reflects scheduler behavior and stays comparable across pools.

2026-01-30 (Caleb Johnson): During staging load, saw negative durations in ~0.02% of samples; traced to mixed clock sources in one helper. Please ensure all timestamps use the same time source (steady clock) end-to-end.

2026-02-06 (Sean Gallagher): For on-call, we need a clean panel: “p95 queueing” and “p95 execution” side-by-side. If queueing is the driver, we’ll route to infra/fleet before waking kernel folks. Please ensure units are ms and naming matches dashboard queries.

2026-02-12 (Noah Patel): Confirmed perf-canary regression evaluator can now distinguish: (a) queueing up with stable execution -> capacity/fleet; (b) execution up with stable queueing -> runtime/kernels/scheduler heuristics. This is the core attribution signal we needed for Phase 1 rollout gates.
